query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation of a homogeneous local environment, which enhances the magnetic entropy change and reduces hysteresis losses.
generation.material_initial_state: Rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure
generation.intervention: Tuning the composition of the alloy by adding FCC metal additives, such as Pd, to optimize the magnetic entropy change and reduce hysteresis losses
generation.conditions: Low applied fields, temperature range of 100 K to room temperature
generation.structural_mediator: Homogeneous local environment, reduced distribution of exchange energies
generation.mechanism: Indirect exchange interaction via conduction electrons, parallel (FM) spin alignment of like and unlike FM neighbors
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced magnetic entropy change, reduced hysteresis losses, and improved mechanical stability
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 100 K to room temperature, applied fields up to 5 T
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the magnetocaloric response and the optimal composition of the alloy are still uncertain and require further investigation

The calculations indicate that (RuNiFeMoCr)3O4 exhibits a Ru-site distribution more favorable for forming homogeneous local environments, which is thermodynamically consistent with the observed trend of enhanced structural stability (figs. S26 to S28). Electronic structure analysis and free energy calculations compared the (RuNiFeMoCr)3O4 (311) surface with the RuO2 (110) surface (Fig. 5A) (). It should be noted that the calculations in this section are based on representative SQS configurations and idealized static surfaces to extract comparable relative trends, without explicitly accounting for possible surface reconstruction/segregation, dynamic valence-state changes, or electrolyte/potential effects under acidic OER conditions. The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. In this article, an EFA descriptor has been developed for the purpose of capturing synthesizability of high-entropy materials. The framework has been applied to refractory metal carbides, leading to the prediction and subsequent experimental discovery of homogeneous high-entropy single phases. The method is able to quantitatively predict the relative propensity of each composition to form a homogeneous single phase, thus identifying the most promising candidates for experimental synthesis. In particular, the experiments validate the prediction that the composition MoNbTaVWC5 should have a very high propensity to form a homogeneous single phase, despite incorporating both Mo2C and W2C, which have different structures (hexagonal and/or orthorhombic instead of rock-salt) and stoichiometric ratios from the five-metal high-entropy material. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that disorder enhances the mechanical properties of these materials: HfNbTaTiZrC5 and HfTaTiWZrC5 are measured to have hardness of 32 GPa (almost 50% higher than the ROM prediction) and 33 GPa, respectively, suggesting a new avenue for designing super-hard materials.
